title: Bounded AI red-team exercise
summary: Plan and conduct an authorized, scoped AI red-team exercise with explicit stop conditions, evidence requirements, and follow-up actions. This intermediate resource keeps adversarial testing within agreed operational and safety boundaries.
prerequisites: Access to the AI system or approved test environment
An accountable owner who can authorize the assessment
A documented incident and escalation process

sections.title: Answer and source correction
paragraphs: How do I run an AI red-team exercise without allowing the assessment to become open-ended or unsafe? Run it only under written authorization, define the permitted system, scenarios, data, participants, timing, evidence handling, stop conditions, and escalation path before testing, and stop whenever those boundaries cannot be maintained. This is an intermediate-level playbook for practitioners who already understand the system being assessed and their organization’s incident process.

The citation record is replaced here with identified NIST sources. This correction affects the source attribution and the basis for authorization, assessment boundaries, documented test conditions, incident handling, and follow-up risk treatment.

A bounded exercise is an adversarial assessment constrained by explicit authorization, scope, roles, limitations, and handling procedures. NIST defines a red team as an authorized group organized to emulate adversary capabilities, while NIST SP 800-115 describes planning elements such as scope, logistics, roles, limitations, data handling, incident handling, and rules of engagement. NIST AI 600-1 applies adversarial testing and red teaming to generative AI risk management and emphasizes documenting test conditions and limitations.
sections.callout: Do not begin testing if authorization, scope, stop authority, evidence handling, or the escalation path is absent or disputed.

sections.title: Bounded exercise procedure
paragraphs: Step 1. Obtain written authorization from the accountable owner. Record the systems and interfaces that may be tested, excluded systems, approved participants, assessment period, permitted data, and who may stop the exercise. If authorization is missing, expired, or disputed, do not test; return the plan to the accountable owner and resume only after the authorization is recorded.

Step 2. Agree on rules of engagement before constructing tests. Define permitted actions, prohibited actions, operational limits, evidence access, communication channels, incident handling, and stop conditions. If a boundary is ambiguous, pause planning and obtain a written decision from the accountable owner. If no owner can decide, defer the exercise rather than interpreting the boundary yourself.

Step 3. Select scenarios that represent the risks being assessed and can be executed within the approved boundaries. For each scenario, record its purpose, input conditions, expected safe behavior, observations to capture, and the condition that ends the test. If a scenario requires prohibited data, unapproved access, or uncontrolled impact, remove or redesign it. If the necessary observations cannot be captured, revise the evidence plan before execution rather than treating an unobservable result as valid.

Step 4. Execute one approved scenario at a time and record the test conditions, inputs, observed behavior, relevant limitations, and time of observation. If a stop condition is reached or unexpected operational impact appears, halt the scenario, preserve the evidence already authorized for retention, and follow the documented escalation or incident process. If required evidence is missing or corrupted, mark the result invalid and repeat the scenario only after evidence collection is restored and renewed execution remains authorized.

Step 5. Triage each observation as supported, unsupported, or requiring further investigation, and connect supported findings to an accountable owner and follow-up action. If reviewers cannot reproduce or agree on a finding, retain the conflicting evidence and label the finding unconfirmed; perform another bounded test only if authorization permits it. If no owner accepts a supported finding, escalate it through the governance path instead of closing it without treatment.

sections.title: Expected evidence and verification
paragraphs: Expected evidence consists of the written authorization, approved scope and rules of engagement, named roles and stop authority, scenario records, documented test conditions, captured observations, limitations, findings, incident or escalation records where applicable, and assigned follow-up actions. Evidence must distinguish what was observed from what was inferred and must not include data that the authorization prohibits retaining.

Verify procedural success by comparing the execution record with the authorization and rules of engagement. Confirm that every executed scenario was approved, every required field was recorded, no excluded system or prohibited data was used, each triggered stop condition has a corresponding halt and escalation record, and every supported finding has an owner and next action. If any check fails, mark the exercise incomplete, correct the missing authorization or evidence, and rerun only the affected scenario when doing so remains safe and authorized.

Verify assessment results separately from procedural success. A completed procedure does not establish that the AI system is safe; it establishes that the recorded findings were produced under the documented conditions and boundaries. Reproduce material findings within the same approved conditions when feasible, record results that do not reproduce as unconfirmed, document test limitations, and track accepted remediation or risk-treatment decisions to closure.
